Neelam: Sorry about lunch 😓 I don't know why I snapped
Arohi: It's ok. You look wrecked though. Did you sleep?
Neelam: Barely. Did the whole physics chapter at night, then scrolled till late
Neelam: I keep crying over nothing and forgetting formulas I KNOW
Neelam: Maybe I'm just a bad-tempered person
Arohi: Or maybe you're just tired. Everything feels huge on no sleep. Happens to me too
Arohi: Can you sleep properly tonight? The chapter will still be there
Arohi: And if you still feel off even after proper sleep, tell your mum or the counsellor, okay?
Neelam: Ugh fine. Phone going in the other room 🙂
Next day
Neelam: Slept. The test wasn't as scary. Thank you 😊

qa.q: What did Neelam do late at night besides studying physics?
qa.a: Neelam scrolled till late.

qa.q: What is Neelam worried about after the snapping, the crying and the forgetting?
qa.a: Neelam worries about being just a bad-tempered person, and says so in the chat.

qa.q: What choice did Neelam make that changed the next day?
qa.a: Neelam put the phone in another room and slept properly, and the test felt less scary.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Neelam's snapping?
qa.a: As tiredness, not a flaw. Arohi says everything feels huge on no sleep and that it happens to Arohi too, and suggests telling a mum or the counsellor if the feeling stays.

grounding: A teenager staying up late finds mood and memory suffering and mistakes tiredness for a flaw.

passage:
In their village near Sangli, Darshan had studied under the solar bulb until past midnight three nights running. On Thursday morning he shouted at his sister Vidya for moving his pen, then sat at breakfast unable to remember the formula he had learned the day before. His eyes filled. "I'm useless," he whispered. "I'm turning into a horrible person."
Amma put down the ladle and looked at his dark eyes. "You're tired, that's all," said Vidya, no longer angry.
"Tonight the light goes off at ten," said Amma. "The books will still be here. And if you still feel like this after proper sleep, we'll speak to your teacher together."
That night he slept, and on the bus next day the formula wandered back like a lost goat.

qa.q: Where did Darshan study at night?
qa.a: Under the solar bulb.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling at breakfast?
qa.a: Ashamed and overwhelmed. His eyes filled, and he whispered that he was useless and turning into a horrible person.

qa.q: What choice did Amma make that helped Darshan?
qa.a: Amma noticed his dark eyes and made the light go off at ten, saying the books would wait, and offered to talk to the teacher if the feeling stayed.

qa.q: How does Vidya see Darshan's shouting after breakfast?
qa.a: Vidya stops being angry and sees it as tiredness. She says, 'You're tired, that's all.'

grounding: A teenager short of sleep becomes irritable and foggy and thinks it is a personality flaw.

passage:
Madhuri, I owe you an apology for yesterday, and an explanation. I've been sleeping maybe five hours a night for two weeks. Chemistry till midnight, then I scroll till one-thirty because it's the only time that feels like mine. Then the alarm at six-thirty.
And I've turned into someone I don't like. I snapped at Mummy about the tiffin. I cried in the bathroom because I got a seven instead of a nine on a quiz, which is ridiculous. And yesterday, when you joked about my hair, I basically bit your head off.
I thought I was just becoming a horrible person. Then on Saturday I slept till ten by accident, and the whole day I was fine. Normal. Nice, even.
So it's not me. Well, it's me, but it's me on no sleep. I'm Darshan, and I'm trying a phone-in-the-kitchen rule at eleven.

qa.q: What score did Darshan get on the quiz?
qa.a: A seven instead of a nine.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel about the snapping and crying before Saturday?
qa.a: Darshan felt ashamed and confused, believing the cause was becoming a horrible person.

qa.q: Why is the phone-in-the-kitchen rule a good step?
qa.a: It cuts the late scrolling so Darshan sleeps more, and Saturday showed that rest makes the whole day fine.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt when Darshan snapped over the hair joke?
qa.a: Madhuri was probably hurt and surprised, having only been joking.

grounding: Shows a teenager staying up late becoming irritable and teary, and mistaking lost sleep for a personality flaw.

passage:
Monday. Jatin had gone to bed at 2 am after gaming, and at school he stared at the whiteboard as if it were in another language. When Lalremsiami Ma'am asked him to read aloud, he slammed the book and said, "Why always me?"
Wednesday. After class Ma'am kept him back. "You're not usually like this. How are you sleeping?" Jatin shrugged, then admitted it: two, sometimes three. She didn't lecture. "Try one week of midnight. Then tell me how Monday feels."
The next Monday. Jatin had been in bed by twelve all week. He read his paragraph aloud, stumbled on one word, laughed at himself and kept going.

qa.q: When had Jatin gone to bed before that first Monday?
qa.a: At 2 am, after gaming.

qa.q: Why did Jatin slam the book and snap at Ma'am?
qa.a: He was exhausted and irritable from going to bed at 2 am, so a small request felt like too much.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She asked about sleep instead of scolding, and suggested one week of midnight bedtimes as a test.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami Ma'am read the slammed book?
qa.a: Ma'am saw it as unusual for Jatin and wondered about tiredness rather than simple rudeness.

grounding: Shows a teenager's late nights making him foggy and reactive, and more sleep bringing back his steadier self.

passage:
Akash, you think you invented staying up late? At fifteen I read novels under the quilt with a torch till two, every night of the monsoon. By August I was a monster. I shouted at my little brother for touching my pencil box. I cried in class because the teacher called my handwriting untidy. My mother thought I had become proud and rude, and I believed her. I thought it was simply who I was.
Then I got the flu and slept for three days straight. When I got up, everything was lighter. My brother, the pencil box, the teacher: none of it seemed worth a tear.
That was when I understood it was not my character. It was the torch. Your Swati Nani put the torch away at ten after that, mostly.

qa.q: What did Swati read under the quilt with a torch?
qa.a: Novels.

qa.q: What did young Swati believe about her own moods?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, believing her mother that she had become proud and rude, as if it were her character.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed Swati's understanding?
qa.a: Sleeping for three days with the flu made everything feel lighter, showing the moods came from the torch-lit nights, not her character.

qa.q: How did Swati's mother see the change in her?
qa.a: Her mother thought Swati had become proud and rude, without seeing the lost sleep behind it.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose late nights made her irritable and tearful, mistaken for a flaw in her character.

passage:
It was the week of the half-yearly exams, and the school bus came at 6:40. Kishore had been awake till two every night, half revising, half watching cricket clips under the blanket.
By Wednesday, everything felt wrong. He read the same chemistry line five times. When his sister Gopika asked to borrow his calculator, he snapped, "Can't you get your own for once?" and then felt terrible. At lunch he nearly cried because the canteen had run out of samosas.
"What's wrong with me?" he muttered. "I'm becoming a horrible person."
Gopika, still annoyed, looked at the dark rings under his eyes. "You're not horrible. You're just not sleeping. You were exactly like this last year."
That night, grudgingly, he put the phone in the kitchen and slept at ten-thirty. Thursday wasn't perfect. But the chemistry made sense, and he laughed at Gopika's joke at breakfast.

qa.q: What time did the school bus come?
qa.a: The school bus came at 6:40.

qa.q: What was Kishore worried about when he muttered "What's wrong with me?"
qa.a: Kishore felt ashamed and frightened that his snapping and near-tears meant he was becoming a horrible person.

qa.q: What small change helped Kishore, and why?
qa.a: Putting his phone in the kitchen and sleeping at ten-thirty, because his irritability and fog came from lost sleep, not his character.

qa.q: How did Gopika see Kishore's mood that week?
qa.a: Gopika was annoyed at first but understood it as tiredness rather than him being horrible, since she'd seen it the year before.

grounding: A teenager staying up late becomes irritable, foggy and reactive, mistaking sleep debt for a personality flaw.
